name: Pure Polynucleotide (PDRN)

angle.text: PDRN is an injectable salmon-derived skin booster borrowed from wound-care medicine and promoted for skin quality, scars and aging signs. Lab and orthopaedic data are promising, while controlled evidence for facial appearance is limited.

summary: Injectable salmon-DNA-derived 'skin booster' borrowed from wound-care medicine; promising lab and orthopaedic data, but little controlled evidence for facial appearance.
note: Most human trials concern wounds and tendons, not cosmetic outcomes; injectable procedure performed by clinicians.
currentQuick:
PDRN, short for polydeoxyribonucleotide, is a mixture of DNA fragments, today mostly purified from salmon or trout reproductive tissue. It was first used in medicine for wound and tissue repair and is now marketed in several countries as an intradermal 'skin booster' meant to improve skin quality, scars and fine lines.
In appearance circles it is discussed as a regenerative alternative or add-on to hyaluronic acid boosters. Published human trials so far mostly cover wounds, tendons and joints, with cosmetic trials only recently registered.
How it works: Laboratory work indicates PDRN is broken down into components including adenosine, which acts on the A2A receptor and is linked to increased blood-vessel growth and tissue repair signalling. Proponents say this translates into better skin quality; this has not been established in large controlled facial trials.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects in the trials surveyed are generally minor, and purified products are described as having low immunogenicity. Regulatory status varies by country and product (medicine in some, device or cosmetic in others). Injection-site reactions and the usual risks of intradermal procedures apply.
deepLead:
Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) is a mixture of single-stranded DNA fragments that was first isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and is now mainly purified from salmon or trout sperm. It is used in wound-healing and tissue-repair medicine and, particularly in parts of Asia and Europe, as an injected cosmetic 'skin booster' marketed for skin quality, scars and aging signs.
Laboratory research describes PDRN as acting through adenosine A2A receptor signalling, with effects on angiogenesis and inflammation. Human trials have studied it mainly for diabetic ulcers, tendon problems and osteoarthritis rather than facial appearance. Cosmetic studies, including scar and periocular wrinkle trials, are registered but small and recent.
In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-procedure discussion it appears as a 'salmon DNA' or polynucleotide option alongside hyaluronic acid boosters.

name: Volite / Volift

angle.text: Juvéderm Volite (VYC-12, also sold as Skinvive) is injected into the skin for smoothness and hydration rather than volume. Trials exist, mostly single-arm and manufacturer-linked.

summary: Juvéderm Volite is a low-concentration hyaluronic acid gel injected into the skin for smoothness and hydration; trial data exist but are mostly single-arm and manufacturer-linked.
note: Volift is a separate product name; the skin-quality gel is Volite. Evidence is mostly single-arm or manufacturer-linked.
currentQuick:
Juvéderm Volite (also marketed as Skinvive, with the gel called VYC-12) is a crosslinked hyaluronic acid gel placed in the skin rather than beneath it, aiming to improve smoothness, hydration and fine texture rather than add volume. Volift is a different product in the same Juvéderm family, a filler used for lines and folds.
It is discussed in aesthetic circles as a 'skin booster' that can be paired with botulinum toxin or fillers. Published studies include a prospective single-arm study, a retrospective cohort and a small randomised split-face trial.
How it works: Clinicians describe injecting small amounts of gel into the dermis at several points, where the hyaluronic acid binds water and is intended to improve surface smoothness and hydration. Volite is described as a lower-concentration, longer-lasting gel than older boosters.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mainly injection-site reactions such as swelling, redness and bruising. Hyaluronic acid fillers carry rarer risks including lumps, delayed inflammatory reactions and vascular complications. It is a clinician-administered, regulated device.
deepLead:
Juvéderm Volite is a crosslinked hyaluronic acid (HA) gel (VYC-12, also marketed as Skinvive) injected intradermally to improve skin quality attributes such as surface smoothness and hydration. It is described as providing longer-lasting effects at a lower HA concentration than traditional fillers.
In a prospective single-arm study, patients with moderate or severe cheek skin roughness received VYC-12 in the cheeks and other areas, and the authors reported it as safe and effective for improving facial skin topography. Other published work includes a Brazilian retrospective cohort, a randomised split-face trial combined with botulinum toxin, and several registered manufacturer-sponsored trials.
Volift is a separate Juvéderm product name; the sources reviewed contain no clinical data on it specifically.

name: Restylane Vital / Skinboosters

angle.text: Restylane Vital is the longest-studied skin booster, used for elasticity and texture. Evidence for this use comes mostly from small clinical studies.

summary: Galderma's small-dose hyaluronic acid injections placed in the skin to improve elasticity and texture; the longest-studied skin booster, mostly in small clinical studies.
note: Most studies are small and several are single-arm; effects are described as temporary.
currentQuick:
Restylane Vital is a stabilised hyaluronic acid gel (NASHA) made by Q-Med/Galderma that is injected as many tiny deposits in the skin to improve its quality, such as elasticity and hydration, rather than to add volume. It sits at the centre of the 'skin booster' category.
Studies since 2008 have measured changes in elasticity and appearance on the face, neck, hands and elsewhere, generally in small groups. In Korea the technique is also called hydrofilling.
How it works: Clinicians place small amounts of gel in the mid-dermis with a needle, a cannula or a specialised injector. The hyaluronic acid binds water and is described as improving hydration and elasticity.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are usually temporary swelling, redness, bruising and small lumps. A case report describes persistent nodules on the neck after HA filler. Hyaluronic acid fillers carry rarer risks such as granulomas and vascular complications, and the procedure is performed by clinicians.
deepLead:
Restylane Vital, part of the Restylane Skinboosters line, is a stabilised hyaluronic acid-based gel of non-animal origin (NASHA) injected into the dermis in small amounts to improve skin quality such as elasticity and smoothness. Restylane is made by Galderma and was the first hyaluronic acid filler approved by the US FDA for cosmetic injection into facial tissue.
The 'skin booster' concept developed as hyaluronic acid products were repurposed from volume filling to dermal conditioning. A 2008 study reported rejuvenating effects on facial skin, and a 2010 pilot measured skin elasticity after three sessions in 19 patients. Later work covers the nasojugal groove, neck, hands and acne scars.
The technique has been described by Wikipedia as having been popularised by a 2007 'fern pattern' approach from Dutch doctor Tom van Eijk to restore dermal elasticity.

name: Redensity

chain: HA gel fills lines and hollows
angle.text: Teoxane's Redensity hyaluronic acid products are used for fine lines and under-eye hollows, with the smoothing visible after the gel is placed. Evidence includes a randomised 52-week perioral trial.

summary: Teoxane's 'Redensity' hyaluronic acid products (RHA Redensity and Teosyal Redensity) for lines and under-eye hollows; includes a randomised 52-week perioral trial.
note: Name covers several different products (a filler for dynamic lines and a under-eye gel); evidence differs by product.
currentQuick:
Redensity is a name used by Teoxane for hyaluronic acid products. RHA Redensity is a 'resilient' HA filler designed for dynamic areas of the face, studied for perioral lines and infra-orbital hollows; Teosyal PureSense Redensity 2 is used for the tear trough under the eyes.
In aesthetic discussion it appears mostly in connection with under-eye and lip-line treatment.
How it works: The gels are injected under or into the skin where hyaluronic acid adds support and hydration. The RHA range is described as made with a process meant to preserve HA structure so the gel stretches and returns with facial movement.
Risks and caveats: Typical reported effects of HA fillers include swelling, bruising and lumps; vascular and delayed inflammatory reactions are rarer. HA fillers can be dissolved with hyaluronidase, and a 2023 study tested response of 21 fillers.
deepLead:
Redensity refers to hyaluronic acid (HA) products from Teoxane, including RHA Redensity (a 'resilient' HA filler) and Teosyal PureSense Redensity 1 and 2.
A randomised, evaluator-blinded multicenter study of RHA Redensity for moderate-to-severe dynamic perioral rhytides ran for 52 weeks against no-treatment control, with the aim of demonstrating superiority. A prospective observational study of Redensity 2 in the periorbital region examined real-world efficacy and safety.
Other work covers laboratory studies of non-crosslinked Redensity 1 as a cell carrier in burn management, cannula delivery for skin density, and responsiveness to hyaluronidase.

name: Sunekos

angle.text: Sunekos is an Italian biorevitalising booster used for photoaged face skin, the eye area and lax skin on thighs, knees and arms. Support is mainly small manufacturer-linked trials.

summary: Italian injectable that mixes hyaluronic acid with amino acids as a skin 'biorevitalising' booster; supported mainly by small manufacturer-linked trials.
note: Few published trials; most registered studies are small and have no posted results in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Sunekos is an injectable that combines hyaluronic acid with amino acids in an alkaline solution, offered in clinics as a skin booster for photoaging, under-eye circles and body skin laxity. The idea is that amino acids supply building blocks for the skin's collagen and elastin.
The published evidence found is thin: one multicenter cellulite study of 46 women, plus registered small studies on face, under-eyes and body.
How it works: Clinicians inject the mixture into or beneath the dermis at several points. Proponents say the amino acids support fibroblast activity; the published research located does not test this mechanism directly.
Risks and caveats: The cellulite study assessed safety alongside efficacy. As with other injectables, local reactions such as swelling and bruising are expected; long-term safety data are limited.
deepLead:
Sunekos is a commercially available mixture of hyaluronic acid and amino acids in an alkaline solution, injected for skin aesthetics. Registered studies have evaluated it for face photoaging, the area around the eyes and skin laxity of the inner thighs, knees and arms.
A 2026 prospective multicenter study evaluated the mixture for cellulite (edematous fibrosclerotic panniculopathy) in 46 women using an injection technique, reporting on efficacy and safety.

name: Exosome facial

angle.text: Exosome facials are used after microneedling or laser to improve skin quality, texture and scarring. Evidence for the appearance use is small early studies, and no exosome product is FDA-approved.

summary: Skin-quality treatment using cell-derived vesicles after microneedling or laser: only small early studies exist and no exosome product is FDA-approved.
note: FDA reported serious adverse events with unapproved exosome products in 2019.
currentQuick:
An exosome facial applies or injects a product said to contain exosomes, tiny vesicles released by cells, usually after microneedling or laser. It is marketed for skin quality, texture and acne scars.
Evidence so far consists of small registered studies, mostly of 7 to 40 people. No large controlled trial was identified.
How it works: Exosomes can carry RNA and proteins between cells, and proponents propose that products from stem-cell or other sources signal skin cells to repair tissue. Most supporting research is from cell and animal work.
Risks and caveats: The FDA stated in 2019 that no exosome products were approved and reported serious adverse events in patients given unapproved exosome-labelled products. Product sources and quality vary between providers.
deepLead:
An exosome facial is an aesthetic procedure in which a product marketed as containing exosomes, small membrane-enclosed vesicles released by cells, is applied to or introduced into the facial skin, commonly after microneedling or laser treatment, with the aim of improving skin quality, texture and scarring.  Exosomes are one subtype of extracellular vesicle, and the source cells for aesthetic products vary: mesenchymal stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord, and plants have all been named in trial registrations. 
In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-clinic circles the treatment is positioned as a next-generation alternative to platelet-rich plasma and similar regenerative procedures. Published evidence is early: the entries found are small registered studies, many with 7 to 40 participants, and several are listed as completed without published results in the record reviewed. 
The US Food and Drug Administration stated in a 2019 public safety notification that no exosome products were FDA-approved, and reported serious adverse events in patients treated with unapproved exosome-labelled products in Nebraska.

name: Mesogun

chain: Skin receives HA, vitamins or PRP
angle.text: A mesogun delivers mesotherapy solutions such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP across the face for glow and hydration. Evidence specific to the device is sparse.

summary: Handheld multi-injector for mesotherapy that delivers small intradermal doses of hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP; device-specific evidence is sparse.
note: Cosmetic mesotherapy has not been tested in standard clinical trials per Wikipedia; infection clusters have been reported.
currentQuick:
A mesogun is a handheld device that fires many tiny injections into the skin quickly. It is used in mesotherapy to deliver substances such as hyaluronic acid, vitamins or PRP, mostly to the face.
Research specific to the device is limited to a lab delivery study, a hydration study and a few case reports.
How it works: A spring or pressure mechanism pushes small amounts of solution into the dermis at each press, avoiding repeated manual injections. A lab study on ink in foam and pig skin examined how the fluid is delivered.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include a rosacea flare after an injection through a stamp-type microneedle and infection clusters after mesotherapy in Australia. Regulation of what gets injected varies by country.
deepLead:
A mesogun is a handheld, spring- or pressure-driven injector used in mesotherapy to deliver many small intradermal injections of a solution in quick succession, typically across the face.  The solutions used in aesthetic practice include hyaluronic acid, vitamins, and, in some clinics, platelet-rich plasma. 
Mesotherapy itself is described by Wikipedia as an alternative-medicine technique that injects drugs, enzymes, vitamins, plant extracts or hyaluronic acid just below the skin, and notes that cosmetic uses have not been tested in standard clinical trials.  Published work specifically on mesogun devices is small: a laboratory study of delivery behaviour, a trial of a stamp-type microneedle injector for skin hydration, and case reports including an adverse reaction.

name: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections

angle.text: PRP is used for skin rejuvenation, wrinkles, under-eye areas and hair, and is often paired with microneedling as a vampire facial. Trial evidence is mostly from knees rather than faces.

summary: Centrifuged-blood injectable used for skin and under-eye rejuvenation; trial evidence is mostly from knees, not faces.
note: A 2024 CDC report linked an unlicensed spa's vampire facials to three HIV diagnoses.
currentQuick:
PRP is made by spinning a person's own blood to concentrate platelets, then injecting or applying it. In aesthetics it is marketed for skin rejuvenation, hair and under-eye areas.
Most controlled trials are on knee osteoarthritis and other joint problems, with mixed results. Facial studies are small case series.
How it works: Platelets contain growth factors and cytokines thought to promote tissue repair. PRP is often applied with microneedling or injected with fine needles or mesotherapy devices.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects are low in most trials per Wikipedia, but the CDC reported HIV diagnoses linked to an unlicensed spa reusing contaminated equipment. PRP is not itself FDA-regulated; use is off-label.
deepLead:
Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma prepared from a person's own blood. The blood is centrifuged to remove red cells while retaining platelets, which contain growth factors and cytokines thought to aid tissue healing.  The concentrate is then injected or applied to the target area. In aesthetic medicine it is marketed for wrinkles, skin rejuvenation and hair growth, and it is sometimes combined with microneedling in what is popularly called a 'vampire facial'. 
In looksmaxxing forums, PRP is discussed mainly for under-eye hollows and dark circles, often compared with hyaluronic acid tear-trough filler.  Most of the clinical research on PRP concerns knee osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal conditions rather than facial appearance, with mixed results. 
The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so clinical use is off-label, while the devices used to prepare it need clearance.

name: PRF (platelet-rich fibrin)

chain: Own fibrin clot placed under eyes
Lighter dark circles, fuller eye area
angle.text: Forum users try PRF for dark under-eye circles and eye bags, and some report mixed results. It is established in dental surgery, and no facial trials were found.

summary: Fibrin-clot cousin of PRP used in dental surgery and tried by forum users for under-eye circles; no facial trials found.
note: Published trials are dental; forum reports on dark circles are mixed.
currentQuick:
PRF is made by spinning a person's own blood without anticoagulant so that platelets and white cells are trapped in a fibrin clot. It is mainly a dental and oral surgery material for healing.
On looksmax.org some users try it for dark under-eye circles, with mixed reports and no published trials for that purpose.
How it works: Activated platelets in the fibrin matrix release growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF and EGF, which is thought to support tissue healing.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia does not discuss risks. Under-eye injection and homemade serums have no controlled safety data in the sources reviewed. PRF preparation falls under an FDA product code that is 510(k) exempt.
deepLead:
Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), also called leukocyte- and platelet-rich fibrin (L-PRF), is a derivative of platelet-rich plasma in which a person's own platelets and white blood cells are held in a fibrin matrix. Blood is drawn without anticoagulant and centrifuged immediately, producing a clot layer between platelet-poor plasma and red cells.  A 2006 series of papers by Dohan, Choukroun and colleagues described it as a 'second-generation platelet concentrate'. 
PRF is used mainly in oral and maxillofacial surgery for socket preservation, sinus lifts, periodontal regeneration and regenerative endodontics.  In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an under-eye treatment for dark circles and eye bags, and as a component of DIY or clinic-made facial serums.  Published trials in the sources reviewed are dental; none examined under-eye appearance.

name: Liquid facelift

chain: Fillers placed in several face areas
angle.text: A liquid facelift is the marketing term for combining fillers, often hyaluronic acid, in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery, with the change visible immediately. The literature is mostly reviews.

summary: Marketing term for filler-based non-surgical facial rejuvenation; the literature is mostly reviews, with no controlled trials found.
note: Rare filler complications include vascular embolization and vision loss.
currentQuick:
A liquid facelift uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, in several facial areas to restore volume and contour without surgery. The phrase is a marketing term and is also used for one surgical water-jet technique.
The sources found are narrative reviews and a 25-patient surgical case series, not controlled trials.
How it works: Fillers are placed to replace volume lost with aging in facial compartments. Most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months according to Wikipedia.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are bruising, redness and pain. Rare but serious risks include infection, lumps, vascular embolization and permanent vision loss. Fillers are FDA-regulated medical devices.
deepLead:
'Liquid facelift' is a marketing term for non-surgical facial rejuvenation that uses injectable fillers, often hyaluronic acid, to restore volume and contour in several areas of the face in one session.  The term is also used in one 2018 case series for a different technique: water jet-assisted liposuction used alongside surgical rhytidectomy. 
Injectable fillers are classified by the US FDA as medical devices. Wikipedia reports that most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months, and lists bruising, lumps, infection and, rarely, vision loss from vascular embolization among risks.

name: Collagen induction therapy

angle.text: Microneedling or dermarolling is used for acne scars, wrinkles and texture, and is often combined with PRP or topicals. Scars are the best-studied use, with more modest evidence for wrinkles and texture.

summary: Microneedling: controlled skin punctures meant to trigger collagen repair; the best-studied use is scars, with more modest evidence for wrinkles and texture.
note: Non-clinical settings with poor infection control have been linked to blood-borne infection outbreaks when combined with blood-derived products.
currentQuick:
Collagen induction therapy, usually called microneedling, uses a roller, stamp or motorised pen studded with fine needles to puncture the skin many times. The aim is to provoke a wound-healing response that produces new collagen and elastin without removing the epidermis.
It is used for acne and other scars, stretch marks, fine lines, skin laxity and general skin texture. Published studies, mostly small or retrospective, report improvement in scars and some photoaging, while larger controlled evidence is more limited.
How it works: Needle punctures create micro-channels and tiny injuries in the dermis. Proponents and authors of the early clinical papers describe a healing cascade of inflammation, fibroblast activity and new collagen deposition over weeks to months, with the epidermis left largely intact.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include redness, swelling, pinpoint bleeding and temporary irritation. Infections, pigment changes and scarring have been described in complication reviews, and public-health authorities have warned about blood-borne infection when needling is paired with blood-derived products in unregulated settings. Professional microneedling devices are regulated as medical devices in the US; home devices vary widely.
deepLead:
Collagen induction therapy (CIT), widely known as microneedling, dermarolling or skin needling, is a cosmetic procedure in which a device bearing fine needles repeatedly punctures the skin to create controlled micro-injuries . The intended result is stimulation of the skin's repair processes and new collagen and elastin formation, as an alternative to ablative treatments that remove the epidermis .
It is used for acne and other scars, stretch marks, wrinkles, photoaging and skin laxity, and is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a skin-quality and scar treatment. Published clinical work includes retrospective series, small trials and case reports describing improvement in scars, burn scars, striae and upper-lip wrinkles .
Reviews of procedural complications and later literature note that evidence quality varies, that device and protocol standardisation is lacking, and that infection-control failures in non-clinical settings have caused harm .

name: Aqualyx

angle.text: Aqualyx is a deoxycholate injectable sold in Europe for localized fat, and forum users discuss it for facial hollowing and slimming. That facial use goes beyond clinical evidence, and claims of permanence are anecdotal.

summary: A deoxycholate injectable sold in Europe for localized fat; its use for facial hollowing in forums goes beyond any clinical evidence.
note: Not FDA-approved; counterfeit and DIY use have been associated with infection and nodule reports.
currentQuick:
Aqualyx is a CE-marked injectable made from deoxycholic acid, a bile acid that dissolves fat cell membranes. In Europe it is sold to trained practitioners for reducing small pockets of fat such as under the chin.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to slim the cheeks, jaw and neck area. Published clinical evidence for these uses is limited to small studies and case reports, and no published trial has tested facial-hollowing as described in forums.
How it works: Deoxycholate acts as a detergent on fat cell membranes, causing cells to break open; the body then clears the debris, with inflammation and later fibrosis described in the treated area. The related drug Kybella is the US-approved deoxycholic acid product for submental fat.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are swelling, bruising and pain. A published case described chronic infection and nodule formation after a deoxycholate injection. The product is not FDA-approved, counterfeits have been discussed in forums, and the manufacturer sells only to trained professionals; self-injection is outside labelled use.
deepLead:
Aqualyx is a gel-like aqueous solution of sodium deoxycholate, developed in Italy by Professor Pasquale Motolese and commercially available since 2009, marketed by Marllor and sold to doctors and nurses trained in intralipotherapy . It is CE-marked in the European Union and used for localized subcutaneous fat .
Deoxycholic acid is a naturally occurring bile acid; the US FDA has approved a different deoxycholic acid product, Kybella, for submental fat . Aqualyx has no FDA approval .
Published studies of Aqualyx are limited. One empirical study examined ultrasound-guided injection for lipomas , and a case report described chronic infection and nodules after a deoxycholate injection . In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for slimming the lower face and neck, an application no published trial has evaluated.

name: Follicular unit extraction (FUE)

angle.text: FUE is a hair transplant method that restores density to receding or thinning areas and avoids a linear donor scar. The restored hair is visible once grafts grow in, at the cost of longer surgery.

summary: Hair transplant method that removes follicles one by one from the donor scalp, avoiding a linear scar at the cost of longer surgery.
note: Results depend on the surgeon; ongoing native hair loss may require further procedures.
currentQuick:
Follicular unit extraction is a hair transplant technique in which small circular punches remove individual follicular units, usually one to four hairs, from the back and sides of the scalp. They are then implanted in thinning or bald areas.
It was introduced in the early 2000s as an alternative to strip harvesting (FUT), which leaves a linear scar. Descriptions in the literature cite tiny scattered scars instead, though outcomes depend on technique and patient.
How it works: Grafts taken from the donor zone keep their genetic resistance to pattern hair loss, a principle called donor dominance, so transplanted hair is described as long-lasting. Extraction is done under local anaesthetic, with grafts placed into small recipient incisions.
Risks and caveats: Described effects include temporary swelling, temporary shedding of transplanted hair (shock loss), folliculitis, numbness, transected follicles and, in rare cases, scarring. Over-harvesting can leave a thinned donor area, and native hair loss can continue after surgery.
deepLead:
Follicular unit extraction (FUE) is a hair restoration technique in which individual follicular units are removed from the donor scalp with small punches, instead of excising a strip of skin, and transplanted to areas of hair loss . The term was coined in a 2002 paper that introduced the approach as minimally invasive surgery for hair transplantation .
Wikipedia describes FUE as using 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches under local anaesthesia, leaving small scattered scars and shorter recovery, while noting drawbacks of longer surgery time, higher cost and a steep learning curve . Robotic systems have been developed to assist, with US approvals reported for NeoGraft in 2009 and ARTAS in 2011 .
FUE is a major topic in hair loss and hairline discussions, including variants such as sapphire FUE and DHI.

name: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT)

chain: Scalp strip taken from donor area
angle.text: FUT, or strip harvesting, is a hair transplant technique that moves donor hair to thinning areas, producing visible new density and leaving a thin linear donor scar. It is the older of the two main harvest methods.

summary: Strip-harvest hair transplant: a scalp strip is removed and dissected into grafts, leaving a thin linear donor scar.
note: Leaves a linear donor scar, which is the main reason many patients choose FUE instead.
currentQuick:
Follicular unit transplantation removes a thin strip of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which technicians dissect under microscopes into natural follicular units for implanting in balding areas.
It became the standard hair transplant approach in the 1990s and is often compared with follicular unit extraction (FUE), which avoids a strip incision.
How it works: Grafts from the donor zone retain resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hairs are described as lasting. The strip method allows many grafts from a single session, with the wound closed by sutures.
Risks and caveats: The donor site retains a thin linear scar that is usually concealed by surrounding hair. Recovery includes stitches or staples and about two weeks of healing; shock loss and other graft-related effects are described.
deepLead:
Follicular unit transplantation (FUT), also called strip harvesting, is a hair transplant technique in which a strip of scalp is taken from the donor region and divided under stereo-microscopes into follicular units for implantation . Wikipedia describes strip excision as replacing plug grafts in the 1980s, with microscopic dissection of strips developed in the late 1980s .
The procedure leaves a thin linear scar that is typically hidden by hair; a 2002 paper introducing FUE described donor scarring after strip excision as infrequent but concerning enough to warrant an alternative .

name: Direct hair implantation (DHI)

angle.text: DHI is an FUE variant using an implanter pen, promoted by clinics for precise placement and density. The transplanted hair is visibly restored, while independent comparisons with other methods are scarce.

summary: A FUE variant that places grafts with a pen-style implanter; clinics promote precision, but independent evidence is scarce.
note: Reported to be costlier and slower than standard FUE; no controlled studies were found.
currentQuick:
Direct hair implantation uses a hollow pen-like implanter, associated with the Choi pen, to place extracted follicular units directly into the scalp without pre-cut recipient slits. It is a variant of follicular unit extraction.
Clinics that offer it say it allows control of angle and direction, particularly at the hairline.
How it works: Follicles are extracted as in FUE, loaded into the implanter and inserted in a single step. Grokipedia describes creating the site and placing the graft together.
Risks and caveats: Grokipedia reports longer surgery, higher skill requirements, fewer grafts per session and higher costs than standard FUE; risks are those of FUE generally, including swelling, folliculitis and transection.
deepLead:
Direct hair implantation (DHI) is a hair transplant technique using the Choi implanter pen to implant follicular units without separate pre-made incisions . It follows FUE-style extraction of follicles from the donor scalp.
According to Grokipedia, proponents cite greater control of angle and direction and suitability for delicate areas such as the hairline, while drawbacks include longer procedures and costs reported at 40 to 60 percent above standard FUE . These claims come from an AI-generated source, and no controlled comparison was found.

name: Sapphire FUE

angle.text: Sapphire FUE is promoted as giving finer incisions, denser placement and faster healing for hair transplants. The hair restoration itself is visible, while independent evidence for the sapphire-blade advantage is limited.

summary: FUE variant using sapphire-tipped blades for recipient incisions; promoted as finer, with little independent evidence yet.
note: Advantages are largely claimed by clinics; one 2026 comparison study exists.
currentQuick:
Sapphire FUE is a variant of hair transplantation in which recipient channels are cut with sapphire blades rather than steel ones.
Clinics describe finer incisions that may allow denser placement and faster healing; evidence comparing the two blade types is limited.
How it works: Follicles are extracted as in standard FUE, then implanted into channels made with sapphire-tipped blades, which Grokipedia describes as sharper with incisions of about 0.5 to 1.0 mm.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of FUE in general, such as swelling, shock loss and folliculitis. A registered trial examined a topical agent for wound healing after sapphire FUE.
deepLead:
Sapphire FUE is a follicular unit extraction hair transplant in which recipient sites are made with sapphire blades instead of steel . Grokipedia says the blades are sharper and finer, which may allow denser placement, less bleeding, faster healing and less visible scarring ; these are unverified descriptions from an AI-generated source.
A 2026 paper compared sapphire and steel FUE blades alongside forceps methods and treatment times , and a registered trial studied topical rifamycin SV for wound healing after sapphire FUE .

name: Choi implanter pen

chain: Pen makes incision and places graft
angle.text: The Choi implanter pen is the tool behind DHI, used to place follicular units in a single step during hair transplants. Clinics promote its precision, and published comparisons are absent.

summary: A pen-style implanter that places each graft as the incision is made; clinics promote it, but published comparisons are absent.
note: Claims about survival and density come from clinics and general references, not trials.
currentQuick:
The Choi implanter pen is a tool used in some hair transplants to open the recipient site and insert a follicular unit in one step. It is the basis of the technique often marketed as DHI.
Clinics say it gives better control of angle and depth. Reference sources also note higher cost, longer procedures and fewer grafts per session.
How it works: Follicular units are extracted individually (FUE), loaded into the hollow pen, and implanted directly without pre-made slits.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of FUE hair transplantation generally, such as swelling, folliculitis, scarring and poor graft take. No trials were found comparing the pen with other implantation methods.
deepLead:
The Choi implanter pen is a hand-held device used in hair transplantation to make the recipient-site opening and place a harvested follicular unit in a single step. It is most often associated with the technique marketed as Direct Hair Implantation (DHI), described as a variant of follicular unit extraction (FUE) in which grafts are loaded into the pen rather than placed into pre-cut slits.
Clinics that offer pen-based implantation say it gives control over the angle, direction and depth of each graft and shortens the time grafts spend outside the body. Reference sources describe the approach as typically more expensive and slower than conventional FUE, with fewer grafts per session and results that depend heavily on the surgeon. The Wikipedia article on hair transplantation does not cover the pen itself, and no controlled trial comparing pen implantation with other placement methods was identified in the sources reviewed.

Scalp reduction cuts out a strip of bald scalp and stitches hair-bearing skin together to shrink the bald area. It has been described in surgical journals since at least 1980, often alongside hair transplants.

deepLead:
Scalp reduction is a surgical procedure in which a segment of hairless or thinning scalp skin is cut out and the remaining hair-bearing scalp is pulled together and sutured, reducing the area of bald skin. In the dermatologic literature it was described as an adjunct to hair transplantation as early as 1980.
Related published work includes serial reductions analysed biomechanically, scalp extension techniques, a device for managing suture tension during skin closure, and use of the procedure for a skull condition, cutis verticis gyrata. The Wikipedia article on hair transplantation does not describe scalp reduction, and no controlled trials were found.

ARTAS is a robot from Restoration Robotics that finds and extracts donor hair follicles during FUE hair transplants. It was reported cleared by the FDA in 2011 for men.
It automates harvesting only; implantation still involves the surgical team. Registered trials compare it with manual harvest.
How it works: Imaging maps the donor scalp and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units.

deepLead:
The ARTAS system is a computer-assisted robotic device for hair restoration, made by Restoration Robotics. It uses image guidance to identify and extract individual follicular units from the donor scalp in follicular unit extraction (FUE).
Reference sources report US FDA clearance in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with androgenetic alopecia, and describe a system using high-definition imaging and a dual-needle punch. Reported drawbacks include higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators. ClinicalTrials.gov lists manufacturer-associated studies comparing computer-assisted and manual harvest, but no results were available in the sources reviewed.

deepLead:
NeoGraft is an automated device used for follicular unit extraction (FUE) in hair transplantation. Wikipedia describes it as the first robotic surgical device FDA-approved for hair restoration, in 2009, while noting limited detail. Grokipedia describes it as using pneumatic pressure to extract and deliver grafts without twisting or pulling.
A surgeon abstract presented in 2014 argued that most hair-restoration patients are not appropriate FUE candidates, whether extraction is manual or done with NeoGraft or the ARTAS robot. No published trial comparing NeoGraft with other harvesting methods was identified.
